items.title: 68357_Jimmy Maxwell oral history interview
items.q: people like Fred Waring and a lot of other people fought commercial use of recordings

ctx.x: No, they've completely phased us out, you know. Automation took over. You know, the jukeboxes, the TV sets in the bars. And I guess the bars had to have the TV sets because if they didn't, people would stay home and not come to the bars.

I think, though, that the downfall of everything started with recordings. In the '20s and '30s, people like Fred Waring and a lot of other people fought commercial use of recordings, public use of recordings. And when the union conceded that, or didn't do enough -- and again, I put everything on the union and the union means the membership, too. You know what a divided membership we've got. If we'd ever had any solid kind of action and got something done in Congress about it -- there was something done. It says…
That's true. They played those things on all the stations. But now they don't even have that little circle on the record that says, this is for home consumption only. When did that disappear?
